lessons.title: Give each ready process a turn
lessons.intro: A long burst need not monopolize an interactive system. Round Robin limits a turn and returns unfinished work to the queue so other ready processes can run.
lessons.why: Queue order and remaining burst determine the Gantt chart. A time quantum is a maximum turn, not an instruction to waste time after a process finishes.
lessons.definition: Round Robin schedules a ready queue in cyclic order, giving each selected process up to a time quantum q before preemption if it still has work.
steps: Take the head of the ready queue. Run it for min(q, remaining burst), unless the model includes a blocking event that ends the burst sooner.
If it finishes, record completion and do not requeue it. If it remains runnable after q, append it to the queue tail.
Add newly arriving processes according to the stated arrival policy. At exactly simultaneous arrival/quantum boundaries, specify event order if it affects the result.
A very large q approaches FCFS behavior. A very small q improves turn-taking but increases switching frequency and overhead.
With n continuously ready processes and no overhead/new arrivals, a process waits at most (n−1)q between turns. This simplified bound is not universal for dynamic queues and nonzero overhead.
Use separate response and waiting calculations. Round Robin often improves initial responsiveness while average turnaround may be worse than SJF.

example.question: All arrive 0: P1=24, P2=3, P3=3; q=4, order P1,P2,P3, zero overhead.
example.answer: P1 0–4; P2 4–7; P3 7–10; P1 10–14,14–18,18–22,22–26,26–30. Completions are 30,7,10. Waiting is 6,4,7 (average 5.67); response is 0,4,7 (average 3.67); turnaround averages 15.67.

misconceptions: A process with 2 units remaining uses only 2 units even if q=4.
After the other jobs finish, consecutive quanta of the same process need not imply useful switches to another process.
The lecture’s timing ranges are illustrative, not a universal OS specification.
lessons.recall: What is the main cost of choosing q extremely small relative to switch time?
lessons.recallAnswer: A large fraction of elapsed time is spent switching rather than advancing application work.

lessons.title: Different classes can use different policies
lessons.intro: Interactive work and long background jobs have different needs. A scheduler can organize ready work into several classes instead of forcing one policy on every task.
lessons.why: You must distinguish scheduling inside a queue from scheduling between queues, and fixed queue membership from feedback-based movement.
lessons.definition: Multilevel queue scheduling partitions work into queues with separate policies. Multilevel feedback queues additionally permit migration between queues based on defined rules.
steps: A fixed multilevel design assigns each process to a queue, such as foreground interactive or background batch work.
Each queue has an internal algorithm: for example foreground Round Robin and background FCFS.
A between-queue policy decides which queue receives CPU time. Strict queue priority can starve lower queues; allocating a time share to each queue provides a different trade-off.
Feedback queues move processes based on behavior or waiting. A process that consumes its full time slice may be demoted; aging or periodic boosts can promote waiting work.
The source example has Q0 with q=8, Q1 with q=16 and Q2 using FCFS. To calculate an exact timeline, admission, promotion, demotion and between-queue rules must also be specified.
Changing queues is the defining distinction of feedback, not simply having several queues with different names.

example.question: A scheduler gives foreground RR 80% of CPU time and background FCFS 20%. Is this the same as strict foreground priority?
example.answer: No. The time-share policy reserves a portion for background work; strict foreground priority can leave background work with no service while foreground remains ready.

misconceptions: Several queues do not automatically make a feedback scheduler.
Knowing only the quantum of each queue is insufficient for a unique MLFQ timeline.
Aging must be defined as a rule, not merely named.
lessons.recall: What extra rules must an MLFQ design specify beyond per-queue algorithms?
lessons.recallAnswer: Initial placement, when to promote or demote, and how the CPU is allocated between queues; also tie and arrival handling for exact calculations.

lessons.title: Balance the machine without losing locality or deadlines
lessons.intro: With several cores, “which process next?” becomes “which process on which core?” For real-time work, finishing after a deadline may be unacceptable even if average throughput is high.
lessons.why: The scheduling PDF includes both multiprocessor and real-time sections, so its coverage extends beyond the six classic single-CPU algorithms.
lessons.definition: Multiprocessor scheduling distributes work across processors. Real-time scheduling considers timing constraints; hard real-time tasks require deadlines to be met, while soft real-time favors timely service without that guarantee.
steps: Asymmetric multiprocessing assigns central system decisions to a designated processor in the source model. Symmetric multiprocessing lets processors participate in scheduling and execution.
Load balancing seeks to avoid an idle core while another is overloaded. Push migration moves work from a busy processor; pull migration lets an idle processor take waiting work.
Processor affinity preserves locality by keeping work near cached data. Soft affinity is a preference; hard affinity restricts execution to an allowed processor set.
Balancing and affinity can conflict: migration may use an idle core but lose useful cache locality. NUMA and heterogeneous processors add memory-access and capability considerations.
A memory stall means execution waits for data. Hardware multithreading or scheduling other ready work may improve resource use, but ordinary OS switches are not the only mechanism.
Interrupt latency runs from an interrupt event to the start of its handler. Dispatch latency covers moving CPU control to the selected task. Both affect event response.

For hard real-time behavior, average speed is insufficient: worst-case timing, scheduling policy and workload feasibility matter. The source’s soft real-time definition prioritizes critical work without guaranteeing its deadline.

example.question: A task is pinned to core 0 while core 1 is idle. Why might it still wait?
example.answer: Hard affinity can prohibit execution on core 1. Relaxing affinity may improve balance, but migration can lose cache locality. If the task has a deadline, the timing effect must be assessed rather than assuming an idle core fixes it.

misconceptions: More cores do not eliminate scheduling policy.
Processor affinity is not the same as a permanent private CPU.
High priority alone does not prove a hard deadline will be met.
lessons.recall: What is the difference between interrupt latency and dispatch latency?
lessons.recallAnswer: Interrupt latency is delay until interrupt handling starts; dispatch latency is the handoff delay to the task selected for execution.

lessons.title: A single increment can contain several steps
lessons.intro: Two pieces of code can each be correct in isolation and still produce a wrong result when their operations interleave over shared data.
lessons.why: The lecture’s counter example shows why a source-code statement such as counter++ is not necessarily atomic. You must reason about loads, computation and stores.
lessons.definition: A race condition occurs when a result depends on uncontrolled timing/interleaving of concurrent access. A bounded producer-consumer buffer has finite capacity, so producers wait when full and consumers wait when empty.
steps: Represent a circular buffer with in and out positions. Advance each modulo N so the indices wrap. A count can record the number of occupied slots.
A producer creates data, waits for space, writes a slot and updates bookkeeping. A consumer waits for data, reads a slot and updates bookkeeping.
A typical increment is load counter into a register, add one, store it back. A decrement similarly loads, subtracts and stores. The operations can be interleaved.
Starting at count=5, producer and consumer can both read 5. The producer computes 6; the consumer computes 4. If stores occur 6 then 4, the final count is 4 instead of the correct net 5.
Reversing those final stores can leave 6. Both results lose one update. Executing each entire update with suitable synchronization preserves the intended net result.
Single-core preemption is enough to create this problem; multiple cores are not required. Atomicity, ordering and shared access must be designed explicitly.

example.question: Starting counter=5, P reads 5 and computes 6; C reads 5 and computes 4; C stores 4; P stores 6. What is final value and correct net value?
example.answer: The final stored value is 6, but one increment and one decrement should net to 5. The final producer store overwrites the consumer’s update.

misconceptions: One source-code line is not necessarily one atomic machine operation.
Concurrency on one CPU can still cause races.
Checking “not full” or “not empty” alone does not protect shared bookkeeping.
lessons.recall: Why is counter++ unsafe when unsynchronized concurrent code also modifies counter?
lessons.recallAnswer: Its read/modify/write steps can interleave with another update, so one final store may overwrite an update based on an earlier value.

lessons.title: Exclusion alone is not enough
lessons.intro: A door that never opens prevents two people entering together, but it is not a useful access policy. Correct synchronization must allow progress as well as prevent conflicts.
lessons.why: The three critical-section requirements test different failure modes. Explain each separately rather than treating “no race” as a complete answer.
lessons.definition: A critical section accesses shared state that must be protected against conflicting concurrent access. A correct solution aims for mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under its stated assumptions.
steps: The entry section obtains permission; the critical section performs protected work; the exit section releases permission; the remainder section performs unrelated work.
Mutual exclusion means at most one participant executes the protected critical section for the shared resource at a time.
Progress means that if the critical section is free and participants want to enter, the decision about the next entrant cannot be postponed indefinitely by unrelated/nonparticipating work.
Bounded waiting limits how many other entries can occur after a participant requests entry before it is admitted. It addresses indefinite postponement.
Strict alternation using only turn can ensure exclusion but violate progress: a process may have to wait for the other’s turn even when the other does not want to enter.
These properties require assumptions about atomic operations, memory ordering and execution opportunities. A synchronization algorithm cannot make a permanently unscheduled process execute by itself.

example.question: Only P0 wants the critical section, but turn=P1 and P1 stays in its remainder section. Which requirement does strict alternation violate?
example.answer: Progress. The section is free and P0 wants to enter, yet P1’s nonparticipation prevents P0’s admission. Mutual exclusion may still hold.

misconceptions: Mutual exclusion does not automatically imply bounded waiting.
A busy wait is not proof that progress is impossible; correctness depends on the protocol.
Unrelated critical sections for independent resources need not all share one global lock.
lessons.recall: How does bounded waiting differ from mutual exclusion?
lessons.recallAnswer: Mutual exclusion prevents simultaneous protected entry; bounded waiting limits how many others can go first after a request, preventing indefinite bypass under the model.

lessons.title: Express intent, then yield priority
lessons.intro: If two processes both want a protected region, they need to express interest and break a tie. Peterson’s algorithm uses a flag per process plus a shared turn variable.
lessons.why: The algorithm is a reasoning exercise under an ideal memory model. Its textbook proof is not permission to paste ordinary unsynchronized variables into modern concurrent code.
lessons.definition: Peterson’s solution is a two-participant mutual-exclusion algorithm using flag[2] for intent and turn for tie-breaking, assuming atomic accesses and sequentially consistent ordering.
steps: For process i with other process j: set flag[i]=true to announce intent, then set turn=j to give the other priority if it also wants entry.
Wait while flag[j] && turn==j. If the other does not want entry, or priority now favors i, enter the critical section.
On exit set flag[i]=false, then execute the remainder section.
If both want entry, turn has a single final value, so only one of the two waiting conditions permits entry. Under the model this establishes mutual exclusion.
If one does not want entry, its flag is false and the interested process can proceed. Intent flags therefore avoid strict alternation’s progress failure.

Under its assumptions the protocol also provides bounded waiting between the two participants. Plain-language or compiler/CPU reordering can invalidate those assumptions; production implementations need correct atomics and memory-order guarantees.

example.question: P0 sets flag[0]=true, turn=1; P1 sets flag[1]=true, turn=0. Both flags remain true. Who can enter first?
example.answer: P0 can enter because its wait condition requires turn==1, which is false. P1 waits because flag[0] is true and turn==0. The final turn write favors P0 in this interleaving.

misconceptions: turn alone is not Peterson’s full solution.
The algorithm is for two participants in the presented form.
Atomic loads/stores without the required ordering are not sufficient for the textbook proof on every modern machine.
lessons.recall: What does flag[i] mean, and why is turn assigned to the other participant?
lessons.recallAnswer: flag[i] announces that i wants entry. Assigning turn to the other resolves simultaneous interest by yielding priority, so the last assignment determines which contender waits.

lessons.title: The lock itself must not race
lessons.intro: Putting “if available” before a shared update looks protective, but two processes can both observe available before either changes it. The acquisition needs an indivisible decision.
lessons.why: The lecture gives simplified lock pseudocode. Its atomicity requirement is essential: a separate check followed by a normal store is not a correct lock implementation.
lessons.definition: A mutex protects a critical section through acquisition and release. A spinlock waits by repeatedly testing a condition rather than blocking the executing thread.
steps: A participant acquires the lock before entering protected work and releases it afterward. All conflicting accesses must follow the same locking discipline.
Acquisition must atomically test and claim availability, typically using supported atomic primitives such as compare-and-swap or test-and-set.
With separate ordinary operations, both P0 and P1 can read available=true, then both write false and enter. This defeats mutual exclusion.
A spinlock consumes execution resources while waiting. It can be appropriate for very short waits in some contexts, but long waits waste CPU and may be harmful on a single core.
Not every mutex spins for its entire wait. Blocking/adaptive mutex implementations can suspend a waiter and use scheduling, so “mutex” and “spinlock” are not universal synonyms.
Release must occur on every intended exit path and use the required ordering so protected updates become visible. Forgetting release can block future work indefinitely.

example.question: Two threads perform “while not available: wait; available=false” using ordinary separate operations. Is the lock necessarily safe?
example.answer: No. Both can pass the availability test before either sets false. The test-and-claim must be atomic, with suitable memory-order semantics.

misconceptions: A Boolean variable alone does not make a correct mutex.
Every mutex need not busy-wait.
Locking only writers is insufficient if readers can observe inconsistent intermediate state.
lessons.recall: Why does a spinlock wait differently from a blocking mutex?
lessons.recallAnswer: A spinlock repeatedly checks while consuming CPU execution; a blocking mutex can put the waiter to sleep until it can be awakened and scheduled.

lessons.title: Count resources, then protect the shared update
lessons.intro: A lock controls one entrant. A semaphore can also represent several available resources, or enforce ordering between activities.
lessons.why: You must state initial values and the order of wait/signal operations. Waiting for data while holding the buffer mutex can prevent the producer from ever providing it.
lessons.definition: A semaphore is a synchronization object manipulated through atomic wait and signal operations. A counting semaphore models available permits; a binary semaphore uses two availability states in the simplified model.
steps: In the course’s nonnegative busy-wait model, wait(S) waits until S>0 then decrements atomically; signal(S) increments atomically. Blocking implementations can use different internal representations and queues.
A counting semaphore initialized to k allows up to k permits to be acquired. Each completed use should return the appropriate permit; incorrect extra signals can corrupt the resource count.
A binary semaphore can implement exclusion, but it is not identical to every mutex: mutexes normally include ownership rules, while semaphores are also used for cross-thread signaling.
For a bounded buffer of N slots, initialize empty=N, full=0 and mutex=1. The producer waits on empty, then mutex, inserts an item, signals mutex, then full.
The consumer waits on full, then mutex, removes an item, signals mutex, then empty. empty/full track availability; mutex protects buffer bookkeeping.
Do not acquire mutex and then block waiting for full/empty in a way that prevents the other side from changing the condition. Ordering of waits is part of correctness.
Atomic semaphore operations alone do not guarantee fairness, absence of deadlock or correct application logic; those depend on the complete protocol and implementation.

example.question: A buffer has N=3, currently two items, with no operation in flight. What are full and empty? What happens to them after one successful consume?
example.answer: Initially full=2 and empty=1. A consume obtains one full permit and later signals empty, leaving full=1 and empty=2. The mutex protects the actual removal and index updates.

misconceptions: Semaphore wait is a synchronization operation, not the process-termination wait() call.
A binary semaphore and an owner-tracking mutex are not interchangeable in every API.
Atomic primitives cannot repair an incorrect ordering of resource acquisition.
lessons.recall: Why should the consumer obtain a full permit before taking the buffer mutex?
lessons.recallAnswer: If it held the mutex while waiting for an item, a producer needing that mutex could be unable to insert one, producing deadlock in that design.

lessons.title: No progress for a cycle, or no turn for one waiter
lessons.intro: Two people each hold an object the other needs and refuse to release it. Elsewhere, one person keeps losing a place in line while everyone else proceeds. These are different failures.
lessons.why: The source’s board/marker example illustrates deadlock; priority scheduling illustrates starvation. Define the mechanism rather than only saying “waiting forever.”
lessons.definition: Deadlock is a state in which participants cannot progress because each awaits a resource/event dependent on another in the blocked set. Starvation is indefinite postponement of a participant while other work may continue.
steps: In the source analogy, Sandy holds the board and needs the pen; Kevin holds the pen and needs the board. Neither releases what the other needs, so the pair cannot progress.
A lock-order example is P0 holding A while waiting for B and P1 holding B while waiting for A. Acquiring shared locks in a consistent global order can prevent this particular circular pattern.
Starvation can occur when higher-priority work continually bypasses a lower-priority process or a synchronization queue repeatedly favors others.
Aging or suitable fair queuing can reduce starvation; adding fairness does not automatically fix circular resource dependencies.
Busy waiting is an implementation behavior, not itself proof of deadlock. A spinner may eventually acquire a lock; a blocked process may be part of either normal waiting or a deadlock.
Diagnose who holds what, who waits for what, and whether any participant can perform the release needed to unblock the others. Then identify the specific policy or ordering change.

example.question: P0 holds lock A and waits for B; P1 holds B and waits for A. A third unrelated process keeps running. Is the pair deadlocked or merely starved?
example.answer: The pair is deadlocked because each waits for a release the other cannot reach. The unrelated process making progress does not remove the deadlock among P0 and P1.

misconceptions: Deadlock need not freeze every process on the whole machine.
Starvation can happen without a circular wait.
High CPU utilization does not prove every process is making progress.
lessons.recall: Can one process starve while the rest of the system keeps completing work?
lessons.recallAnswer: Yes. Starvation concerns indefinite postponement of that participant; others can continue receiving resources.

accuracyNotes: Kernel residency is not continuous CPU execution.
A mode switch does not necessarily cause a process switch.
The base/limit length convention uses an exclusive upper bound; an upper-address convention must be stated separately.
The single-threaded process model does not prohibit multithreaded parallel execution.
Cascading termination is an OS-dependent policy; Unix orphan reparenting is not the same as a zombie.
Threads may need kernel services for creation, blocking and synchronization despite user-space shared-memory communication.
The course uses trap/exception/software interrupt terminology broadly; architecture-specific terminology varies.
Scheduling waiting=C−A−B is used only for single-burst/no-I/O examples.
SJF optimality is stated with known bursts and appropriate availability assumptions.
Preemptive-priority ties require an explicit policy; the source example does not fully state one.
Peterson’s textbook proof requires sequentially consistent ordering; ordinary unsynchronized variables are unsafe in modern implementations.
The lecture mutex pseudocode must be interpreted as atomic acquisition, not a separate plain check and store.
Semaphores and mutexes can differ in ownership and signaling semantics.
